lines.text: Now say you want to run code you don't trust: a script from the internet, or code an AI agent just wrote.
You want to put it in a box.
The first kind of box is a container, like Docker.
The kernel shows the code its own files, its own processes, its own network. It looks like a machine of its own.
But every container on the machine talks to the same kernel.
One bug in any of its system calls, and the code is out of its box: in the host, and in every other container.
The second kind of box is a virtual machine.
The code gets a kernel of its own, running on pretend hardware: a processor, memory, a disk and a network card.
Today's processors run this at almost full speed. In Linux, the part that drives them is called KVM.
The code in the box can wreck its own kernel. The real one stays out of reach.
A container is a room in a shared house. A virtual machine is a house of its own.
